title: Israeli categories
hook: most Israelis describe themselves as secular, traditional, religious or Haredi

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: many doors. Conversion differs from stream to stream, and the Torah's welcome is as one born among you. Whom did you welcome? This week: renewal, Jewish without theism, secular and Jewish, still here, different answers, many doors. Today, the week ends in Israel. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

Ask an Israeli about religion, and the answer may not be the name of a movement at all. Often it is one of four Hebrew words. A taxi driver says one. The woman in the next seat on the bus says another. A soldier home for the weekend says a third, and the young man in the black coat at the corner says the fourth. Four words. They describe how a person lives. They are today's word.
screen: `NOT A MOVEMENT'S NAME.` →`FOUR HEBREW WORDS.` → `HOW A PERSON LIVES.`

segments.voice: Israeli categories. Take them one word at a time. First, hiloni: secular. Some readers hear in it chol, the ordinary, the weekday, the opposite of holy. The Torah tells the priests to "put difference between holy and unholy," and in Hebrew that unholy is chol. As Shabbat ends, the Havdalah blessing praises God who separates holy from ordinary. A hiloni Israeli lives mostly on the ordinary side of that line, in Hebrew, with the Bible as the people's story, and may still light candles at Hanukkah or sit at a seder. Second, masorti: traditional, keeping what is handed down. A masorti Israeli keeps some of it, often Friday night and the festivals, without keeping all of it. Careful: Masorti is also the name of the Conservative movement in Israel, but as a word about yourself it simply means traditional. Tomorrow we stay with this middle. Third, dati: religious. Some readers hear in it dat, the word the book of Esther uses for the king's law. A dati Israeli keeps halakha. Some dati Jews call themselves dati leumi, national religious, the Religious Zionists we met earlier this block. Fourth, haredi, the Haredi communities from earlier in the block; the name echoes Isaiah's words to those who tremble: "ye that tremble at his word." Here is the turn: these are words people choose for themselves. They overlap. Someone can be hiloni and fast on Yom Kippur. Someone masorti can pray every morning. The lines are blurry on purpose, because they describe lives, not membership cards. So when a taxi driver answers with one word, it carries a whole way of living.
screen: `HILONI: THE ORDINARY SIDE.` · `MASORTI: SOME OF WHAT'S HANDED DOWN.` · `DATI: KEEPING THE LAW.` · `WORDS PEOPLE CHOOSE FOR THEMSELVES.` · then, large: `HILONI, MASORTI, DATI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn the Hebrew terms, with your breath. Settle, and breathe. On the next out-breath, say quietly, hiloni. Let the ordinary weekday come to mind. On the next, masorti, and let something handed down to you come to mind. On the next, dati, and think of someone who keeps a whole law with care. On the next, haredi, those who tremble at God's word. Then go round again, slower, until the four words feel like four neighbors rather than four boxes. If you pray, you can hold all four in your prayer. The bell holds the time.

Israeli categories. Hiloni, secular; masorti, traditional; dati, religious; haredi, a name that echoes those who tremble at God's word: four words Israelis use to describe how they live. Today's word.
Your line: hiloni, masorti, dati. Today, describe one thing about how you live in a single plain word, and notice how much that word leaves out. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Israeli Jews may describe themselves as hiloni (secular), masorti (traditional), dati (religious) or haredi, and these self-chosen words shape everyday conversation about schools, neighborhoods and Shabbat.

notes: The outline says 'most Israelis describe themselves as...'; the lesson avoids the statistic and says 'often answered ... with one of four Hebrew words'. howItsDone says 'commonly'; confirm acceptable.

Word origins: hiloni from chol (Leviticus 10:10's ben ha-kodesh u-ven ha-chol; Havdalah's bein kodesh lechol); dati from dat (Esther 1:8, 'the law'); masorti from masoret. These are etymologies; confirm with a standard lexicon.
The teach flags that Masorti is also the Israeli name of the Conservative movement (day 1221); confirm the distinction is fairly put.
Week-end look-back in the review names the week's lines (days 1233–1238).
